Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Mr. Nguyen is a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian man married to his long-time partner and father of three children. He works as a farmer in rural Iowa, where he tends to his crops and livestock every day with the dedication and hard work typical of his community. However, Mr. Nguyen has been grappling with severe psychological distress since his youngest child suffered a life-threatening illness last year. The traumatic event began when Mr. Nguyen noticed that his youngest son was growing increasingly weak and feverish over several days. Despite their best efforts to treat him at home, the boy’s condition worsened rapidly, necessitating an urgent hospitalization. The intensity of the medical interventions, including the sight of tubes and machines attached to his child's small body, left Mr. Nguyen with a haunting memory that continues to plague him. Mr. Nguyen has come to dread the darkness of night, which brings back sudden fragments of the traumatic event. Certain songs on the radio or seeing specific parts of his son’s body now act as powerful triggers, causing intense anxiety and distress. He recalls feeling like he was reliving the frightening moments in the hospital each time these triggers appear, with no sense of differentiation between past and present. When confronted by these triggers, Mr. Nguyen often feels compelled to avoid sleep entirely or stay up until very late. This avoidance behavior is driven by his fear that lying down might lead him back into the dark memories and sensations he experienced during the traumatic event. As a result, he has developed erratic sleeping patterns where he stays awake for long stretches of time, only to fall into fragmented and restless sleep. Mr. Nguyen’s nocturnal vigilance stems from his deep-seated conviction that these triggers—like certain songs or the sight of specific body parts—will inevitably draw him back into the traumatic memories. This belief has fueled a cycle where he avoids people and sleep out of an intense fear that they will reignite those painful recollections. His work as a farmer has been significantly impacted by this pattern. Mr. Nguyen now finds himself avoiding social gatherings with fellow farmers, fearing that songs or conversations might trigger his distress. His irregular sleeping habits have also affected his ability to tend to the farm in the early morning hours, leading to a gradual decline in productivity and an increased sense of isolation from his community. Mr. Nguyen had come to believe that by staying awake and avoiding certain triggers, he could somehow prevent the memories from resurfacing. However, this strategy has only exacerbated his anxiety and led him into a self-reinforcing cycle where he feels increasingly trapped by these fears. What finally brought Mr. Nguyen to seek help was the realization that his daily functioning had deteriorated significantly—he felt overwhelmed by the constant fear and couldn't shake the feeling that his memories were still happening in real time. He is most afraid of losing control over his life, but at the same time, he hopes for a way to reclaim some semblance of normalcy and peace. In therapy, Mr. Nguyen will need support in understanding how his triggers are intertwined with his memory and avoidance behaviors, ultimately creating a cycle that intensifies his distress. With this insight, he can begin to develop healthier coping mechanisms and break the self-reinforcing loop that has dominated his life since the traumatic event.
